issues.legal_issue: Time was not of the essence for the purchaser’s payment obligation, and the seller was not justified in terminating the sale agreement for non-payment by the stated date.
material_facts: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property and set dates for payments and completion, but did not expressly make observance of those dates essential to the parties’ rights.
The purchaser said the sellers had agreed to extend the time for paying the disputed instalment; the sellers did not rebut that account with evidence.
The sellers extended the completion date, including in the correspondence in which they purported to make time essential for payment.
The courts found that the purchaser’s conduct was not a gross default warranting the sellers’ attempt to make time essential.
issues.conclusion: Time was not of the essence, and the sellers were not justified in terminating the agreement on the basis that the purchaser failed to pay the instalment by the stated date.
issues.legal_principle: Whether time is of the essence depends on the parties’ intention, assessed from the contract’s words, the nature of the property and contract, and the surrounding circumstances. Time is generally presumed not to be of the essence in contracts concerning immovable property. The party asserting that it is essential bears the burden of pleading and proving it. A seller who gives notice making time essential must be ready and willing to complete, and the purchaser must have committed a sufficiently gross default to justify rescission. The Court relied on Pollock & Mulla’s Indian Contract and Specific Relief Acts and Jamshed Khodaram Irani v. Burjorji Dhunjibhai.

rule.if: specific_performance_dispute and immovable_property_sale and agreement_does_not_make_time_essential and seller_extended_completion and purchaser_default_not_gross

predicates.specific_performance_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim for specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.immovable_property_sale: The agreement is for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.agreement_does_not_make_time_essential: The agreement does not expressly make observance of its stated time limits essential to the parties’ rights.
predicates.seller_extended_completion: The seller extended the time for completion of the sale.
predicates.purchaser_default_not_gross: The purchaser’s conduct did not amount to a gross default justifying the seller’s attempt to make time essential.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance dispute concerns an immovable-property sale and the agreement does not make time essential, an extension of completion coupled with no gross purchaser default means that time is not of the essence.

issues.legal_issue: The purchaser established continuous readiness and willingness to perform the sale agreement for purposes of obtaining specific performance.
material_facts: The courts found that the purchaser was in a position to raise the funds needed to perform the agreement.
The time to complete the sale had been extended beyond the date on which the sellers purported to terminate the agreement.
The purchaser brought the specific-performance suit soon after the purported termination and continued to assert the agreement rather than abandon it.
There was no evidence that the post-dated cheque had been dishonoured, and the courts found no unreasonable delay in payment.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was ready and willing to perform the agreement, and the courts below were right to decree specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, a purchaser seeking specific performance must establish readiness and willingness to fulfil the agreement. It is sufficient to show that the purchaser remained ready and willing to fulfil its terms, did not abandon the contract, and kept it subsisting. The Court relied on Nannapaneni Subayya Chowdary v. Garikapati Veeraya.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_could_raise_required_funds and purchaser_did_not_abandon_contract and purchaser_sued_promptly_after_termination and no_unreasonable_payment_delay

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.purchaser_could_raise_required_funds: The purchaser was in a position to obtain the funds needed to perform the agreement.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_abandon_contract: The purchaser continued to assert the agreement and did not abandon it.
predicates.purchaser_sued_promptly_after_terminatio: The purchaser brought suit soon after the seller purported to terminate the agreement.
predicates.no_unreasonable_payment_delay: The evidence did not establish unreasonable delay in payment or dishonour of the tendered post-dated cheque.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, a purchaser who could raise the necessary funds, kept the agreement alive, sued promptly after termination, and did not unreasonably delay payment is ready and willing to perform.

issues.legal_issue: An increase in the value of the property does not, by itself, justify denying specific performance at the appellate stage after the lower courts have granted the decree.
material_facts: The property was in an urban area, and the sellers argued that its price had risen.
The trial court and the appellate court had both granted specific performance before the matter reached the Supreme Court.
The sellers had not entered the witness box or led evidence supporting their allegations.
issues.conclusion: The alleged rise in the property’s price did not justify denying specific performance at this stage, and the Court dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A rise in the price of land may be relevant when a court is considering whether to grant specific performance for the first time, but it is not a relevant factor at the Supreme Court stage when the courts below have already granted the decree. The Court discussed V. Pechimuthu v. Gowrammal and distinguished K. S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan.

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_specific_performa: The proceeding is an appeal after the lower courts have both granted specific performance.
predicates.property_value_increased: The value of the property increased after the sale agreement.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows concurrent decrees granting specific performance, an increase in property value does not by itself justify denying that relief at the appellate stage.
